Heard learned counsel for the petitioners, the learned counsel appearing for the respondent State and the learned counsel appearing on behalf of the O.P.No.2.
2.

In this petition, the prayer has been made for quashing of the entire criminal proceeding including the order taking cognizance dated 18.02.2011 arising out of C.P.Case No.1947 of 2010,
pending in the court of learned Judicial Magistrate, Dhanbad.
3. The complaint case has been lodged alleging therein that complainant is an ex-employee of M/s BCCL retired in the year 2003 as Driver from Area No.IV.
In 1997 M/s BCCL acquired lands of complainant situated at Mouza Pandeydih measuring approximately 23.55 acres.

He raised objection before the accused no.1 and accused no.1 assured complainant that BCCL would pay compensation and also provide employment to the dependants of Subir Das vs The State Of Jharkhand And Another .... ... on 8 April, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/150276265/
1 the complainant and on the said assurance M/s BCCL acquired the land of the complainant and started production.

sentences.text: The complainant thereafter met accused no.2 for payment of compensation and employment of his relatives on which the accused number 2 asked the complainant to furnish details so that employment may be provided to them.
The complainant thereafter med accused no.6 who informed that 45 employments would be provided and complainant furnished the details of the said 45 persons in year 2006.
The complainant also met accused no.3 who asked him to meet accused no.6.

On meeting accused no.67 complainant was asked to arrange for Rs.67,000/- for each employment on which complainant collected and paid Rs.30,20,000/- to accused no.6 who also received a money receipt to the complainant.
Complainant after some time met accused no.5 who asked complainant to meet accused no.6 and send him before accused no.5 for consideration of the matter.
Complainant thereafter met accused no.6 who advised complainant to come later on.
Accused no.6 after lapse of some time showed the official letter regarding approval of 45 employments and handed over a photo copy of same to the complainant.

In last month of 2008 complainant came to know that M/s BCCL is not going to provide employment on which complainant met accused no.4 and asked him to return the entire amount taken by accused no.6 on which accused no.4 became aggressive and contacted accused no.6 on mobile phone and asked him to return entire amount.

4. Mr. Mehta, the learned counsel appearing on behalf of the petitioners submits that the petitioners are the officers of M/s B.C.C.L. and he submits that the land in question was acquired in the year 1997 and pursuant to that, the persons in which name the land in question was there, they have already been paid compensation.
He submits that so far as the complainant is concerned, he has got no concern with the said land and falsely the present case has been lodged.
He further submits that the O.P.No.2 himself has instituted the title suit being Title Suit No.113 of 1997 against M/s B.C.C.L and its officers for the same allegation which is still pending.
He submits that if any case is prima facie made out, that is civil in nature.
On this ground, he submits that the entire criminal proceeding may kindly be quashed.
5. The learned State counsel submits that out of complaint case, the present case has arisen and the learned court has taken cognizance.

6. Mr. Birendra Kumar, the learned counsel appearing on behalf of the complainant submits that the land was fraudulently acquired by M/s B.C.C.L and compensation has not been paid to the complainant and rightly the learned court has been pleased to take cognizance.

Looking to the complaint petition it transpires that the allegation is made in the year 1997, 23.55 acres of land was acquired by M/s B.C.C.L whereas the present complaint case has been lodged in the year 2010 alleging that the compensation amount has not been paid to the complainant and for the same allegation the said suit has been instituted by the complainant which is still pending.

If the compensation is not being paid after the acquisition of the land, rightly the suit has been filed and filing of the present criminal case amounts to abuse of the process of law as there is no criminality made out in view of above facts.
For making out a case of cheating a person must deceive the another.

A reference may be made to the case of M.N.G. Bharateesh Reddy v. Ramesh Ranganathan and Another, reported in 2022 SCC OnLine SC 1061 wherein the case between Hridaya Ranjan Prasad Verma v. State of Bihar has been considered by the Hon'ble Supreme Court, paragraph nos.16, 17 and 18 of the said judgment are as follow:
16.

sentences.text: In Hridaya Ranjan Prasad Verma v. State of Bihar, a two-judge bench of this Court interpreted sections 415 and 420 of IPC to hold that fraudulent or dishonest intention is a precondition to constitute the offence of cheating.

entities.text: Hridaya Ranjan Prasad Verma v. State of Bihar
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
The relevant extract from the judgment reads thus:
"14. On a reading of the section it is manifest that in the definition there are set forth two separate classes of acts which the person deceived may be induced to do.
In the first place he may be induced fraudulently or dishonestly to deliver any property to any person.
The second class of acts set forth in the section is the doing or omitting to do anything which the person deceived would not do or omit to do if he were not so deceived.
In the first class of cases the inducing must be fraudulent or dishonest.
In the second class of acts, the inducing must be intentional but not fraudulent or dishonest.
15. In determining the question it has to be kept in mind that the distinction between mere breach of contract and the offence of cheating is a fine one.
It depends upon the intention of the accused at the time of inducement which may be judged by his subsequent conduct but for this subsequent conduct is not the sole test.

Mere breach of contract cannot give rise to criminal prosecution for cheating unless fraudulent or dishonest intention is shown right at the beginning of the transaction, that is the time when the offence is said to have been committed.
Therefore it is the intention which is the gist of the offence.
To hold a person guilty of cheating it is necessary to show that he had fraudulent or dishonest intention at the time of making the promise.
From his mere failure to keep up promise subsequently such a culpable intention right at the beginning, that is, when he made the promise cannot be presumed."
(emphasis supplied)
17. In Dalip Kaur v. Jagnar Singh5 a two-judge bench of this Court held that a dispute arising out of a breach of contract would not amount to an offence of cheating under section 415 and 420.

The relevant extract is as follows:
"9. The ingredients of Section 420 of Penal Code are:

sentences.text: Applying the above principles, the ingredients of Sections 415 and 420 are not made out in the present case.
The grievance of the first respondent arises from the termination of his services at the hospital.
The allegations indicate that there was an improper billing in respect of the surgical services which were rendered by the complainant at the hospital.
At the most, the allegations allude to a breach of terms of the Consultancy Agreement by the Appellant, which is essentially in the nature of a civil dispute.

8. Coming to the facts of the present case, admittedly the allegations are made out for acquisition of land and the compensation was not paid, however, the same has been denied by the petitioners on the ground that the complainant is not the actual owner and the actual owner has already been paid.

Thus, it is a case of civil in nature and rightly civil suit has been filed and filing of the present case is an abuse of process of law.
9.

Accordingly, entire criminal proceeding including the order taking cognizance dated 18.02.2011 arising out of C.P.Case No.1947 of 2010, pending in the court of learned Judicial Magistrate,
Dhanbad are quashed.
10. This petition is allowed and disposed of.
11. Pending petition if any also stands disposed of accordingly.
